steps.title: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, and COUNTA

blocks.text: With a full column of delivery amounts or times, you often want one summary number. SUM adds every value in a range: =SUM(D2:D21) totals all order amounts on your Orders sheet. AVERAGE returns the arithmetic mean: =AVERAGE(C2:C21) gives the average delivery time, skipping blank cells and text but including any cell that contains zero (Pending or Cancelled orders with no recorded time are blank, not zero, so they are excluded).

blocks.takeaway: COUNT returns a smaller number than COUNTA when the column contains blanks or text, because COUNT skips non-numeric cells while COUNTA counts everything that is not empty.

steps.lede: Four functions that reduce a whole column to one summary number.

segments.label: SUM, AVERAGE, and COUNT applied to a range of numbers
segments.summary: The presenter enters =SUM over a column of ten numbers and gets 5,220, then builds =AVERAGE over the same range, pausing to show it is equivalent to dividing the SUM by the COUNT of that range. Finally, =COUNT is applied to the same column, returning 10; deleting one value drops the result to 9, confirming that COUNT only registers cells holding numbers.

blocks.group_title: SUM, AVERAGE, and COUNT demonstrated on a number column

bridge.before: Watch how SUM, AVERAGE, and COUNT are entered and what each returns. Note: COUNTA is not shown here — the text covers it.
bridge.after: The clip confirms COUNT ignores blank cells. The text adds the full rule: COUNT also skips text and logical values, and introduces COUNTA for counting anything non-blank.

steps.title: COUNT vs COUNTA: What Gets Counted

blocks.text: COUNT counts only cells that contain numbers; empty cells, text, and error values are skipped. On your Orders sheet, =COUNT(C2:C21) counts only the rows where delivery_minutes is recorded (Delivered orders) — Pending and Cancelled rows with NULL times are excluded.

COUNTA counts every cell that is not empty, regardless of type — numbers, text, or error values all count. =COUNTA(C2:C21) on the same column returns a larger number than COUNT because it includes any row that has any value at all. Use COUNTA when you need to count rows, not just numeric entries.

steps.lede: The difference matters whenever a column mixes numbers, blanks, or text.

steps.title: Choosing the Right Aggregation Function
steps.lede: Which function should you use for each summarisation requirement?

public.prompt:
The Orders sheet has 20 rows. Column A holds order IDs (text like "LG-2001"), column C holds delivery_minutes (numbers for delivered orders, blank for pending/cancelled), and column D holds order amounts (all numbers).

A manager asks: "How many orders have a recorded delivery time?" Which function should you use, and why?

options.text: COUNT(C2:C21) — because COUNT counts only numeric cells and delivery_minutes is blank for undelivered orders.
COUNTA(C2:C21) — because COUNTA counts all non-empty cells, including text.
SUM(C2:C21) — because SUM adds up all the delivery times to give a total count.
AVERAGE(C2:C21) — because AVERAGE returns the number of values in the range.

opt_b.message: COUNTA counts any non-empty cell, including text. For delivery_minutes, all non-blank cells are numbers, so COUNTA and COUNT give the same result here. But COUNT is the precise choice: it counts only numeric cells, which is exactly what 'has a recorded delivery time' means.

opt_c.message: SUM adds the values together and returns a total number of minutes, not a count of rows. To count how many rows have a value, use COUNT or COUNTA.

opt_d.message: AVERAGE returns the arithmetic mean of the values, not the number of values. To count how many cells contain a number, use COUNT.

correct.message: Correct! COUNT(C2:C21) counts only the numeric cells in the delivery_minutes column. Blank cells (for pending/cancelled orders) are skipped, so the result equals the number of orders with a recorded delivery time.

incorrect.message: COUNT counts only numeric cells and ignores blanks, text, and logical values. Because delivery_minutes is blank for undelivered orders, COUNT(C2:C21) returns exactly the number of orders that have a recorded delivery time.

hints: COUNT counts only numbers. COUNTA counts anything that is not empty. SUM adds values. AVERAGE computes a mean.
Blank cells in delivery_minutes represent orders with no recorded time — COUNT skips them automatically.

steps.title: Summarise the Orders Sheet
steps.lede: Write SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, and COUNTA formulas on the QuickDeliver data.

public.prompt:
The Orders sheet has 20 rows of data (rows 2–21). Column A holds order IDs — text values like "LG-2001". Column D holds order amounts — all numeric.

In cell H1, write a formula using **COUNTA** that counts how many non-empty cells are in the order_id column (A2:A21). Because order IDs are text, COUNT would return 0 — COUNTA is the right choice here.

The expected result is **20**.

correct.message: Correct! =COUNTA(A2:A21) returns 20 because all 20 order-ID cells are non-empty. COUNTA counts any non-empty cell — numbers, text, or errors — while COUNT counts only numeric cells. Since order IDs are text, COUNT(A2:A21) would return 0.

incorrect.message: Use =COUNTA(A2:A21). COUNTA counts every non-empty cell regardless of type, so it correctly counts the 20 text order IDs. COUNT would return 0 here because it only counts numeric cells.

hints: COUNTA counts cells that contain any value — numbers, text, or errors. COUNT counts only numbers.
The range A2:A21 covers all 20 data rows in column A (order_id).

steps.title: IF, Nested IF, AND, and OR

blocks.text: IF tests a condition and returns one value when it is TRUE and another when it is FALSE. Its syntax is IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false). Text results go in quotes: =IF(C2>60,"Late","On Time") placed in a helper column (H) labels each order row based on its delivery_minutes value without overwriting the amount column.

Multiple IF functions can be nested to handle more than two outcomes. =IF(H2>89,"A",IF(H2>79,"B",IF(H2>69,"C",IF(H2>59,"D","F")))) converts a numeric score to a letter grade. The same structure could sort orders into delivery-time bands in a helper column instead of a single Late/On-Time split.

steps.lede: Label, flag, or categorise rows based on conditions — without changing the data.

segments.label: IF with AND and OR: classifying rows by one or two conditions
segments.summary: Using a travel-claims dataset, the presenter builds an IF formula that labels claims as 'high value' or 'standard' based on a single amount threshold, demonstrating that text results must be wrapped in double quotes. AND is then introduced in isolation to show it returns TRUE only when every condition is met, before being placed inside IF's logical-test argument to auto-approve claims that satisfy two criteria at once. OR is introduced next: it returns TRUE when at least one condition is met and FALSE only when all conditions are FALSE, and is used inside IF to calculate a settlement offer for claims meeting either of two criteria. A formula result (a calculation) is shown without quotes, contrasting with quoted text.

segments.label: Nested IF with AND and OR: layering multiple conditions on a revenue list
segments.summary: Working through a list of apps and their revenues, the presenter builds an IF formula argument by argument, noting that text values in formulas require quotation marks and that an empty string ('""') returns nothing. AND is then placed inside IF's logical-test position to check two revenue boundaries simultaneously. A nested IF is constructed by placing a second IF inside the value-if-false argument of the first, producing three outcome bands; the presenter notes that Excel exits the formula as soon as it finds a TRUE condition, so order matters. Finally, OR is used inside IF's logical-test to flag rows that meet either of two threshold conditions.

blocks.group_title: Building IF, AND, and OR formulas step by step in a spreadsheet

bridge.before: Watch how each formula is built argument by argument. Notice where AND and OR sit inside IF, and how a second IF slots into the false branch. Neither clip covers the letter-grade nested-IF pattern from the teaching text.
bridge.after: The clips show the evaluation order clearly: Excel stops at the first TRUE branch. The teaching text covers the letter-grade nested-IF example (f6) that neither clip demonstrates.

steps.title: AND and OR: Testing Multiple Conditions

blocks.text: AND returns TRUE only when all of its arguments are TRUE; if any one is FALSE, AND returns FALSE. Its syntax is AND(logical1, logical2, ...). Use AND as the logical_test of IF to require every condition to hold: =IF(AND(C2>30,E2="Delivered"),"Fast Delivery","Other") flags only orders that are both fast and delivered.

OR returns TRUE when any of its arguments is TRUE; it returns FALSE only when all arguments are FALSE. Its syntax is OR(logical1, logical2, ...). =IF(OR(E2="Pending",E2="Cancelled"),"Not Delivered","Delivered") flags any order that has not yet completed.

steps.lede: Combine conditions inside IF to test more than one thing at once.

steps.title: Reading an IF Formula
steps.lede: Which formula correctly labels an order as "Late" when delivery_minutes exceeds 60?

public.prompt:
Cell C2 holds a delivery time in minutes. You want a formula in F2 that displays "Late" if the delivery took more than 60 minutes, or "On Time" otherwise.

Which formula is correct?

opt_b.message: Text results in an IF formula must be enclosed in double quotation marks. Without quotes, Excel tries to interpret Late and On Time as cell names or named ranges and returns a #NAME? error.

opt_c.message: The logical_test (C2>60) must not be in quotes. Putting it in quotes makes Excel treat it as a text string rather than evaluating it as a comparison, so the condition is never tested.

opt_d.message: The arguments are in the wrong order. IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false): the second argument is returned when the condition is TRUE (C2>60), so "Late" must come second, not "On Time".

correct.message: Correct! =IF(C2>60,"Late","On Time") tests whether C2 is greater than 60. If TRUE it returns the text "Late"; if FALSE it returns "On Time". Text values in formulas must always be wrapped in double quotation marks.

incorrect.message: The IF syntax is IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false). Text results must be in double quotes: "Late" and "On Time". The logical test (C2>60) must not be in quotes — it is a comparison, not text.

hints: Text in a formula always goes inside double quotation marks, like "Late".
The second argument of IF is what is returned when the condition is TRUE.

steps.title: AND vs OR
steps.lede: Write nested IF formulas with AND and OR to classify delivery times.

public.prompt:
The **orders** sheet has delivery times in column C (rows 2–5). You need to classify each delivery into one of three bands:

- **"Late"** if delivery_minutes > 60
- **"On Time"** if delivery_minutes is between 30 and 60 (inclusive on both ends)
- **"Fast"** if delivery_minutes < 30

**Task 1 — nested IF with AND:** In cell F2, write a nested IF formula that classifies the delivery time in C2. Use **AND** as the logical_test of the inner IF to enforce both the lower bound (>=30) and the upper bound (<=60) of the "On Time" band. Then write the same formula in F3 and F4.

Expected results:
- F2: **"Fast"** (C2 = 28)
- F3: **"Fast"** (C3 = 25)
- F4: **"On Time"** (C4 = 56)

**Task 2 — OR flag:** In cell F5, write an IF formula that returns **"Extreme"** if C5 is less than 20 **OR** greater than 70, and **"Normal"** otherwise. Use **OR** as the logical_test.

Expected result:
- F5: **"Extreme"** (C5 = 19)

solution_files.content:
// Input cells (typed constants):
orders!C2: 28
orders!C3: 25
orders!C4: 56
orders!C5: 19

// Formula cells:
F2: =IF(C2>60,"Late",IF(AND(C2>=30,C2<=60),"On Time","Fast"))
F3: =IF(C3>60,"Late",IF(AND(C3>=30,C3<=60),"On Time","Fast"))
F4: =IF(C4>60,"Late",IF(AND(C4>=30,C4<=60),"On Time","Fast"))
F5: =IF(OR(C5<20,C5>70),"Extreme","Normal")

tests.message_on_fail: F2 should be "Fast" because C2=28 is less than 30. Check the order of your IF conditions: test >60 first, then AND(>=30,<=60), then the else is Fast.
F3 should be "Fast" because C3=25 is less than 30. Check the order of your IF conditions: test >60 first, then AND(>=30,<=60), then the else is Fast.
F4 should be "On Time" because C4=56 is between 30 and 60. Use AND(C4>=30,C4<=60) as the logical_test of the inner IF.
F2 must use both IF and AND. Use AND(C2>=30,C2<=60) as the logical_test of the inner IF to enforce both bounds of the 'On Time' band.
F5 should be "Extreme" because C5=19 is less than 20. Use =IF(OR(C5<20,C5>70),"Extreme","Normal"). OR returns TRUE when any condition is met.
F5 must use both IF and OR. Use OR(C5<20,C5>70) as the logical_test: OR returns TRUE when any one of its conditions is TRUE.

correct.message: Well done! Your nested IF correctly classifies all three delivery times using AND for the On Time band. AND returns TRUE only when BOTH conditions are met. Your OR formula in F5 correctly flags C5=19 as Extreme because OR returns TRUE when ANY condition is met (19 < 20 is TRUE).

incorrect.message: For F2–F4: use =IF(C2>60,"Late",IF(AND(C2>=30,C2<=60),"On Time","Fast")). AND requires BOTH bounds to be true. For F5: use =IF(OR(C5<20,C5>70),"Extreme","Normal"). OR returns TRUE when ANY condition is true.

hints: Start with the outer IF: =IF(C2>60,"Late", ...). Then nest another IF for the middle band.
AND(C2>=30,C2<=60) returns TRUE only when C2 is at least 30 AND at most 60.

steps.title: Aggregation and Logical Functions — Key Takeaways
steps.lede: What you've learned in this tile.

blocks.text: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, and COUNTA each reduce a range to one number; which one you reach for depends on whether you need a total, a mean, a count of numbers, or a count of anything non-blank. IF tests a condition and returns different values for TRUE and FALSE; nest IFs for multiple outcomes, and use AND or OR to combine conditions.

blocks.title: Up Next: Text, Date, and Conditional Aggregation
blocks.text: In the next tile you'll combine and extract text with TEXTJOIN and LEFT/RIGHT/MID, calculate date differences with TODAY and DATEDIF, and count or sum only the rows that meet a condition with COUNTIF and SUMIFS.

remediation_steps.title: Matching the Function to the Task

blocks.text: SUM totals numbers. AVERAGE finds the mean (blank cells are skipped, zero-value cells are included). COUNT counts only numeric cells — blank and text cells are excluded. COUNTA counts every non-blank cell regardless of type. On the Orders sheet: use SUM for total amount, AVERAGE for mean delivery time, COUNT for how many deliveries have a recorded time, COUNTA for how many rows have any entry.

IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false) evaluates the test first. If the test is TRUE, the formula returns value_if_true; if FALSE, value_if_false. =IF(C2>60,"Late","On Time"): when C2 is 45, the test 45>60 is FALSE, so the formula returns "On Time". Text values in IF must be wrapped in quotes.

remediation_steps.title: AND Requires All; OR Requires Any

blocks.text: AND(condition1, condition2) returns TRUE only when every condition is TRUE — one FALSE makes the whole AND FALSE. OR(condition1, condition2) returns TRUE when at least one condition is TRUE — it returns FALSE only when every condition is FALSE. Use AND when all criteria must hold; use OR when any one is enough.
